questions.question_text: Which of the numbers below cannot be written as a fraction of two integers?

options.why: Took any square root to be impossible to write as a fraction without checking that $169$ is a perfect square, so $\sqrt{169}=13=\frac{13}{1}$.
Treated a recurring decimal as non-repeating; it repeats, so it equals the fraction $\frac{2}{11}$.
Assumed a fraction that gives the decimal $0.875$ stops being a fraction; a fraction of two integers is always rational.

questions.solution_text:
$\sqrt{169}=13=\frac{13}{1}$ and $\frac{7}{8}$ are already fractions of integers.
$0.\overline{18}$ repeats, so it equals $\frac{2}{11}$.
$21$ is not a perfect square, so $\sqrt{21}=4.58257\ldots$ never stops and never repeats.
$\sqrt{21}$ cannot be written as a fraction of two integers, so it is irrational.

questions.question_text: One of these four numbers is rational. Which one is it?

options.why: Assumed multiplying $\pi$ by a whole number clears the endless non-repeating digits; $2\pi=6.28318\ldots$ is still irrational.
Took $27$ to be a perfect square because it is a perfect cube; it lies between $25$ and $36$, so the root is irrational.
Assumed a minus sign in front makes a root rational; the sign does not change whether the digits stop or repeat.

questions.solution_text:
$\sqrt{16}=4$, so $3\sqrt{16}=12=\frac{12}{1}$, a fraction of two integers.
$3\sqrt{16}$ is rational.

questions.question_text: Which statement about real numbers is correct?

options.text: Every rational number and every irrational number is a real number.
Only rational numbers are real numbers.
options.why: Believes a number with endless non-repeating digits has no position on the number line, when $\pi$ and $\sqrt{2}$ both do.

options.text: Only numbers that can be written as terminating decimals are real.
options.why: Excludes recurring decimals and irrationals, although both can be marked on the number line.

options.text: A number is real only if it is positive.
options.why: Confuses being real with being positive; negative numbers sit to the left of $0$ on the line.

questions.solution_text:
A real number is any number that can be represented by a point on the number line.
Rational numbers and irrational numbers together fill that line, so both families are real.

options.why: Inverted the fraction and located $\frac{5}{14}\approx0.36$ instead.
Divided $14$ by $10$ rather than by $5$, giving $1.4$.
Wrote $14\div5$ as $2$ remainder $4$ and read the remainder as the decimal part, giving $2.4$.
Mixed up the two common approximations, using $1.73$ for the dot instead of $1.41$.
Read the dot as exactly one third of the way from $1$ to $2$, which is $1.33$.

questions.solution_text:
The dot lies between $1$ and $2$, a little before the halfway tick, so it is about $1.4$.
$\sqrt{2}=1.41421\ldots$, which matches that position.

questions.question_text: Between which two consecutive integers does $\sqrt{22}$ lie, and is it rational or irrational?

options.why: Took the perfect square $25$ as the lower boundary instead of the upper one, giving $5$ to $6$.
Located it correctly but assumed every square root can be written as a fraction of integers.
Used $25$ as the lower boundary and also assumed every square root is a fraction.

questions.solution_text:
$4^{2}=16$ and $5^{2}=25$, and $16<22<25$.
$\sqrt{22}=4.69041\ldots$
So it lies between $4$ and $5$, and because $22$ is not a perfect square the decimal never stops and never repeats, so it is irrational.

questions.question_text: Which reason correctly explains why $0.\overline{36}$ is a real number?

options.text: It equals the fraction $\frac{4}{11}$, and every rational number has a point on the number line.
It is not a real number, because its digits never stop.
options.why: Confuses a recurring decimal with a non-terminating, non-recurring one; recurring decimals are rational and therefore real.

options.text: It is real only because it is smaller than $1$.
options.why: Thinks being real depends on size, when every point on the line is real however large or small.

options.text: It is irrational, so it cannot be placed on the number line.
options.why: Believes irrational numbers have no position on the number line, when in fact every irrational number has one.

questions.solution_text:
$0.\overline{36}$ repeats, so it can be written as a fraction: $0.\overline{36}=\frac{36}{99}=\frac{4}{11}$.
Every rational number can be represented by a point on the number line, so $0.\overline{36}$ is real.

questions.question_text: Which number lies between $\sqrt{2}$ and $\sqrt{3}$ and is rational?

options.why: Chose a rational number below $\sqrt{2}\approx1.41$, so it is outside the interval.
Took the midpoint of the numbers under the roots; $\sqrt{2.5}\approx1.58$ is in the interval but is still irrational.
Chose a rational number above $\sqrt{3}\approx1.73$, so it is outside the interval.

questions.solution_text:
$\sqrt{2}\approx1.41$ and $\sqrt{3}\approx1.73$.
$\frac{8}{5}=1.6$, which lies between them.
It is a fraction of two integers, so it is rational.

questions.question_text: How many real numbers lie between $\frac{1}{4}$ and $\frac{1}{3}$?

options.why: Reads $\frac{1}{4}$ and $\frac{1}{3}$ as neighbouring points, as though fractions came in fixed steps like the integers do.
Finds the single midpoint and assumes it is the only number available between them.
Counts only the hundredths $0.26$ to $0.33$, as though the line had no points between hundredths.

questions.solution_text:
$\frac{1}{4}=0.25$ and $\frac{1}{3}=0.333\ldots$
Between any two points on the number line there are infinitely many more real numbers, both rational and irrational.
So infinitely many real numbers lie between them.
